one_liner: Single-header C++11 unit-testing framework whose header and asserts compile far faster than Catch2 v2's single header.
what_it_does: doctest is a Catch-style unit-testing framework (TEST_CASE, SUBCASE, CHECK/REQUIRE, INFO, test suites, decorators, reporters) shipped as one header, with the test runner instantiated in exactly one translation unit via DOCTEST_CONFIG_IMPLEMENT or DOCTEST_CONFIG_IMPLEMENT_WITH_MAIN. Because including the header is cheap, it is designed for writing tests next to production code, even in headers, and DOCTEST_CONFIG_DISABLE strips every test and most of the framework from the binary. Asserts can also be used outside a test context as a general assert library. It is not a build cache: its speed claim is that test code using it compiles faster.
how_it_is_fast: The public part of doctest.h forward-declares what it needs (it even forward-declares std::ostream, std::istream, std::tuple and std::nullptr_t inside namespace std) and pulls no standard headers into user translation units; all the iostream, container and threading includes live only in the implementation TU. Expression-decomposing CHECK(a==b) uses template machinery (ExpressionDecomposer plus a ResultBuilder wrapped in try/catch); DOCTEST_CONFIG_SUPER_FAST_ASSERTS collapses each assert into a single call to an out-of-line, non-inlined function (decomp_assert, binary_assert, unary_assert) with no try/catch, and the binary CHECK_EQ(a,b) form skips expression decomposition entirely. Together these cut per-assert instantiation and code size, which is where the assert-compile gains come from.
when_to_use: Test headers included in many translation units, or tests written inline in production .cpp/.h files: the 2018 run measured 11-23 ms per extra TU for doctest.h against 380-470 ms for Catch 2.3.0's catch.hpp
Replacing a Catch2 v2 single-header (catch.hpp) setup where header cost dominates the test build; the FAQ gives SECTION and tagged TEST_CASE macro shims for migration
Codebases held to C++11/14/17, where [Boost].UT (C++20 only) is not an option
Suites with tens of thousands of asserts where you can switch to CHECK_EQ-style binary asserts and define DOCTEST_CONFIG_SUPER_FAST_ASSERTS (the page's fastest assert-compile configuration)
Shipping tests inside release sources and removing them from the final binary with DOCTEST_CONFIG_DISABLE
when_not_to_use: Already on Catch2 v3 (a compiled library with cheap per-test headers): no benchmark covers it, and issue #1168 (June 2026) reports a 13-file, 1,273-assert executable taking about 30 s with both Catch2 v3.7.1 and doctest 2.5.2 (MSVC 14.44 and GCC 13.1); a maintainer replied that the benchmarks are outdated and that doctest.h now pulls in all of its machinery

Expecting faster test execution for plain asserts: the page shows parity on Linux GCC Release (0.29 s vs 0.29 s for 10M asserts) and a small gap on Clang Release (0.28 s vs 0.32 s); the big runtime wins appear only with INFO() logging

Needing death tests or first-class Google Mock integration (the FAQ lists both as gaps versus Google Test), Catch2's micro-benchmarking, or in-process parallel execution of test cases (test cases run serially; parallelism means launching the binary several times with test ranges)

Generating many SUBCASEs in a loop on doctest 2.5.0-2.5.3: issue #1208 (open) reports super-linear scaling from a linear sibling scan added in 2.5.0, with one reporter's binary going from 112 s on 2.4.12 to 2420 s

Optimized builds with Visual Studio 2026 cl.exe 19.51+: issue #1138 (open) reports some CHECK()/CHECK_UNARY() calls evaluating incorrectly; the reporter attributes it to an MSVC regression and filed it with Microsoft

integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (tag 1.2.9 for C++98); features page (marked partly outdated) lists GCC 4.8-12, Clang 3.5-15 and MSVC 2015-2022 as tested
integration.platforms: Windows, Linux and macOS in CI; any C++11 compiler claimed; Windows SEH and POSIX signal handling are configurable
integration.thread_safety: Assertion and logging macros may be called from multiple threads spawned by one test case; test cases run serially and SUBCASEs must be used only from the runner thread. DOCTEST_CONFIG_NO_MULTITHREADING removes the threading support for single-threaded speed.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — Catch-like macro surface (TEST_CASE, CHECK, REQUIRE, INFO, Approx), but SECTION becomes SUBCASE, Catch tags must be folded into test names, and Catch matchers, BENCHMARK and other features differ; the FAQ supplies a few #define shims for the common cases

gotchas: DOCTEST_CONFIG_SUPER_FAST_ASSERTS implies DOCTEST_CONFIG_NO_TRY_CATCH_IN_ASSERTS: an exception thrown while evaluating an assert aborts the whole test case, and a debugger breaks inside doctest's internal function instead of at the assert line

The default forward declarations of std::ostream, std::tuple and friends inside namespace std are not permitted by the C++ standard; a niche standard library can fail to compile, and DOCTEST_CONFIG_USE_STD_HEADERS fixes it at the cost of including the real headers

Self-registering tests compiled into a static library are dropped by the linker unless something references their object file; use CMake OBJECT libraries, the shipped doctest_force_link_static_lib_in_target() helper, or /OPT:NOREF or /WHOLEARCHIVE on MSVC
char* operands are compared as pointers unless DOCTEST_CONFIG_TREAT_CHAR_STAR_AS_STRING is defined
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against [Boost].UT, pick doctest when you cannot require C++20, want the more widely used Catch-style macro API, or have large multi-file suites, where UT's own benchmark shows doctest compiling as fast or faster except at gcc9 -O3. The cache and distribution tools in this category (ccache, sccache, distcc, FASTBuild and others) are complementary: they cut rebuild cost of any test framework, while doctest cuts the per-translation-unit cost of the test code itself.
verified_claims_summary: The project's own December 2018 benchmark built bench.py-generated CMake projects single-threaded with doctest 2.2.0 and Catch 2.3.0 on an Intel i7 3770k (Windows 7 on SSD with MSVC 2017 15.8 and MinGW GCC 8.1; Ubuntu 17.04 in a VirtualBox VM on HDD with GCC 6.3 and Clang 4.0): including the header in 200 files took 8.71 s vs 87.17 s on MSVC Release and 11.05 s vs 99.48 s on Linux GCC Release, and 50k CHECK(a==b) asserts took 58.73 s vs 448.68 s on MSVC Release but 257.40 s vs 608.94 s on Linux GCC Release (about 2.4x, derived from page data). Runtime of 10M passing asserts was near parity on GCC and Clang Release and several times faster only with INFO() logging.
status_note: Actively maintained (v2.5.3 tagged 2026-07-06, dev branch commits through 2026-10-18; master stops at the v2.5.0 release commit of 2026-03-27), MIT-licensed single header that is trivial to vendor, though maintainers themselves call the benchmark suite outdated and plan to redo it for 2.6.
